utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The witness did make a solemn declaration before, and that continues throughout his testimony. So the witness can sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before we deal with any other matter, the Trial Chamber would like to make one ruling. And I'll give you an opportunity, Mr. Di Fazio. On the statement of Mr. Sabrija Dagovic, which was disclosed to the Defence by the Prosecution. The statement has an exhibit number, and I'll ask the registry assistant to give us the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is C1, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It's a court document admitted for the limited purpose of assisting the Trial Chamber to decide on whether or not the late disclosure has occasioned any prejudice to the Defence. The Trial Chamber has observed that the statement discusses the events in Bosanski Samac prior to the armed conflict and throughout the period of the conflict until the exchange of the maker, Mr. Sabrija Dagovic. There are matters in the statement which have a bearing on the evidence of Esad Dagovic who had already given evidence by the time this statement was disclosed. The Trial Chamber is of the view that the Prosecution did fail to exercise duly -- due diligence in the obligations towards the Defence as provided by the rules. However, the Trial Chamber has not found any evidence of deliberate failure on the part of the Prosecution to disclose the said statement timely to the Defence. The Trial Chamber finds that the Defence has sufficient remedies available to them under the rules during the rest of the trial. The Defence can recall Mr. Esad Dagovic if they so wish? If they choose to do, so they must give notice during the proceedings tomorrow, Thursday, the 2nd of May. In the event that Mr. Esad Dagovic is recalled, the cross-examination will be limited only to the events in the month of April, 1992 in Bosanski Samac. The Trial Chamber will consider the conduct of the Prosecution in these proceedings as part of the overall evaluation of the evidence after the close of the trial. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Do you wish me to continue now with this witness, or to attend to any other matters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. Let's -- let's complete the evidence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I see. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: In chief. After the examination-in-chief, maybe we will deal with the other matters that are outstanding before the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you just give me a moment to gather my papers. I apologise for the delay. I thought I'd be attending to another issue and I will be able to move into this matter straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Dagovic, on the last occasion that we were here, I had asked you a number of questions about life in Bosanski Samac. And you ended up describing a meeting in the Spomen Dom where there was a recruitment exercise for members of the 4th Detachment. Before I return to that topic, I want to just raise one other issue with you about life in Bosanski Samac in the period of time up to December 1992, and that's the issue of telephones. Did you have your telephone service suspended?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When was it suspended and how -- under what circumstances was it suspended?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps a couple of days before the takeover of Bosanski Samac, telephones simply stopped working. They were disconnected?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were you ever able to get resumption of the service?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did the same thing happen to other members of the Bosanski Samac community?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The telephones of Muslims and Croats were disconnected.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can you comment on whether or not the telephone services of Serb members of the community were so affected?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They continued to have a telephone service.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Di Fazio. Could we find out how the witness knows that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That was indeed my -- my next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You heard the Chamber's comment. How is it you find yourself able to make that assertion? I mean by that that Croats and Muslims had their phones cut but Serbs did not.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I talked to most of my Muslim and Croat friends who also couldn't use their phones, just as my family. Whereas Serbs did and said so publicly. My neighbours had a working telephone service. They didn't even hide it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you ever try and use the telephone service between the months of April and December 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When you say that your neighbours had a working service and didn't try to hide it, can you provide the Chamber with any more detail as to what it was that you saw that makes you -- makes you comment in that way.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They openly -- they openly said their telephones were working. And sometimes they would let us use their phone, although that happened very rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I've dealt with that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay. Just one question, then. Mr. Di Fazio, so when the witness said in response to your question, "Did you ever try and use the telephone service between the months of April and December 1992," the answer was no. He was therefore referring to his own phone in his own house? Is that the correct assumption? Because now he says he did use on some occasion the phone of the neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: As Her Honour has pointed out, you a few questions ago said that you didn't try and use any telephone service between April and December 1992, but sometimes they -- and I assume you meant Serb members of the community -- would let you use their phone. Can you reconcile those two answers. Did you or did you not actually use a telephone service at all during the months of April -- during the time from April 1992 to December 1992? And if so, what was the ethnic background of the person whose telephone service you used?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My family used the phone perhaps two or three times, and the telephone belonged to a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on the last occasion, you came to this Chamber to give evidence, we -- I finished asking you questions about a meeting that you attended at the Spomen Dom. And you gave us details about that, you recall. You said that Mr. Zaric was present. You said that there was an invitation extended to the people assembled, and that they would not be required to perform work duty or forced labour if they joined the 4th Detachment. Do you recall that evidence -- giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to ask you this: Did you ever attend any other meetings where a similar topic was discussed?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only at the Spomen Dom.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I take it from your answer, therefore that, there was a second meeting at some stage.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber if you can say whether or not Simo Zaric was present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the second meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. I've finished with the first meeting. I'm now asking you about the second meeting. Was he present there, or can't you recall?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Again, can you tell the Chamber of the ethnic background of the people who attended the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All Muslims and Croats were invited to attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Again, can you tell the Chamber whether or not those Muslim and Croat workers -- sorry. I'm withdraw that. Whether those Muslims and Croats who attended were people who were engaged in forced labour.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Baen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just believe that there was previous ruling by the Chamber that the Prosecution and the Defence are not to use the term forced labour because it's a legal term. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Later on we decided that we will use it and refer to it as a general term, because the Prosecution is aware of the elements that they have to prove before the Trial Chamber can make a finding that indeed that was forced labour. So it won't matter any more to use the term "forced labour."

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And I'm still asking you about the second meeting that you've just mentioned. Can you tell the Chamber what -- what was discussed at this second meeting.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting discussed the same topics as the first meeting. Again, they tried to convince Muslims and Croats to join the army of the so-called Republika Srpska and to take up rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In -- you've just said that the same topics were discussed. In your evidence on the last occasion you came to the Chamber, you said that the -- a proposal was put to the assembled men, namely that if they joined the 4th Detachment they would no longer be required to perform work duty or forced labour, call it what you will. Was this -- was the same invitation extended to you on this occasion, the same deal, so to speak; you go into the 4th Detachment, you don't have to perform forced labour?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And did anyone accept, as far as you can recall, the offer on this second occasion?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember any Muslims or Croats taking up rifles on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, who was extending the offer at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll just get on to that topic very shortly, if I may -- if Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: First of all, who organised the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And now, to be absolutely certain, who extended the offer? If you don't know a name, that's fine. But what I'm interested in, was it a representative of the 4th Detachment who extended the offer?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a representative of the 4th Detachment who made the proposal, but I can't remember his name just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And can you give us any idea of approximately when this second meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall exactly. It might have been in August or September. I can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Earlier in your evidence, you commented that in December of 1992 you stopped performing the work that you had described and that you were mobilised. I want to turn to that topic now. Approximately when did this occur?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In December 1992, roughly on the 24th or the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That was a significant date, wasn't it? A member of your family was exchanged around that time, I believe. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. My mother was exchanged on the 24th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I see. So -- and you described that you were the last family member left after this particular exchange. And about that time you were mobilised; is that the situation?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How did you receive notice of your mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A courier came to my home with a call-up paper which said that I had to report to the military department, that is, their building, the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Was the -- can you recall what was written on the paper? And in particular, can you recall the name of any organisation or entity or body that was issuing this order?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The paper said the Army of Republika Srpska. It said I had to join the Army of Republika Srpska, the VRS. And the signature at the bottom was that of Mr. Bozo Nenkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: This fellow Bozo Nenkovic, do you know what -- any official positions he'd held in the months leading up to December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He worked at the military department, but I don't know exactly what position he occupied.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. So did you do the report?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Tell the Chamber if you considered yourself to have any choice in the matter of reporting or not.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have a choice, because the threat had been made that we would otherwise be detained and sent to Pale, to wage war there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Where did this threat emanate from?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The members of the 4th Detachment, the members of the army. They had made the threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can you recall when they made the threat?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The following day, when we came to the military department. The threat was that if we failed to respond to the call-up, we would be sent to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I see. So the procedure was that you attended at the -- the military department and presumably there were a number of other men in company with you also reporting.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What was the ethnic background of the other men who were also reporting along with you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I see. And it was following this reporting of you Muslims and Croats that the threat was made.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can you recall who actually made the threat?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just told you. Members of the VRS and members of the 4th Detachment. I can't tell you the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it, then, that it was more than one person saying this to you.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Following that, did you report for actual duty?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day when we were standing in front of the military department, it lasted for about half an hour, perhaps a little more. After that, we were put onto trucks and taken away. We didn't know where we were going.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Where did you end up?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We ended up in Brvnik, but we only learnt that on the third day. We hadn't known right away where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I see. But what I'm -- what I'm interested in knowing is this: You reported. Within half an hour, you've been put on a truck and presumably put in an area where there's fighting. Is that a correct assessment of what you've said?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And presumably they didn't tell you where they were taking you. You only learnt that it was Brvnik some days later.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They didn't tell us where they were taking us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: One further question I forgot to ask you about the other men who reported with you. You said that they were all Muslims and Croats. Can you tell the Chamber if they were also people who had been engaged in forced labour along with you in the preceding months.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were you armed once you arrived at Brvnik?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was only when we arrived there that we were issued with weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And what sort of weapons were they?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got a semi-automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How long were you stationed at Brvnik?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day when we got there -- we remained there for five days. We got back home on the sixth day. So we spent there five days in a row.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I think earlier in your evidence you described how eventually you got out of Yugoslavia -- the former Yugoslavia by going to Belgrade and eventually to another part of Europe, out of the Balkans. And I think you said that that took place sometime in 1994. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I left Bosanski Samac in December 1993, and I left Belgrade in August 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: During that year between December 1992 and December 1993 were you engaged in fighting?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Where were you stationed most of that time?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spent the entire time in Brvnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Was it the situation that you would fight for a period of time and then be given some sort of leave and return to Bosanski Samac for short periods of time, for, I suppose, some sort of rest and then return to the front lines?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Again, it may seem an obvious question, but were you exposed to enemy fire and were you engaged in firing yourself -- fighting, in other words, full-blown fighting?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was exposed to gunfire from the other side. But I personally did not take part in the fighting because I avoided shooting at all costs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That brings us to the question of why. Why did you avoid shooting at all costs? What was it that -- why was it that you didn't want to do that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That meant that I would be shooting at my parents, at my people, at my friends. That's why I didn't want to shoot.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And that was your feeling and your sentiment throughout that year, December 1992 to December 1993?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you have any choice in returning to Brvnik to take up this position as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand the question. What do you mean whether I had a choice whether to return to Brvnik or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honours. I believe that there is a mistake in the transcript, because the witness said that he did not want to fire at his brother, at his parents, at his friends. And in the transcript it doesn't say that he did not want to shoot at his brother. It only mentions the parents and the friends and people. So I would ask my learned colleague to ask the witness whether this is correct or not, whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. Yes, we did hear that the word "brother" was included, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That is the answer at --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You've seen it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, I've seen where its absence is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did -- just so that the transcript is correct, Mr. Dagovic, when you answered about not wanting to shoot at your parents, at your people, at your friends, did you include your brother amongst those people?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I did not want to fire at my brother, at my parents, at my people, at my friends. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Let's return to this issue of choice and freedom. You've already commented on what you say was a lack of choice in whether or not to answer the call-up. I'm now talking about the actual act of going to the front line and fighting or at least avoiding trying to fight. Did you have any -- did you feel that you had any choice in leaving Bosanski Samac and returning to the front line?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You've got to try and tell the Chamber why, why that was so. It may seem perfectly obvious to you, but if need be then I want you to tell the Chamber the obvious, please. Tell them why there was no choice.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the entire time we were under pressure. They followed us while we were there. So we had no choice. They followed us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio -- and I apologise if you might be likely to ask this question. The witness has said that he avoided shooting at all costs, as has just now been reiterated. Was a penalty imposed upon him for refusing to fire while under fire from the other side by whoever was the commanding officer in control of the group he was with?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I don't need to repeat that question. It's abundantly clear, Mr. Dagovic. Can you -- can you assist the Chamber on that topic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a penalty. There was a threat of the military court, and I was detained for three days in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: As a result of not shooting?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When did this happen?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly the date, but it was between 1992, 1993, while I was there. So I don't know correctly. I don't know the exact date when that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. I think we need to get some more details about this. How was it that you were detected not shooting at the enemy? Who saw you? Who reported you? Who denounced you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a soldier who had a bunker next to mine, he told on me when we got there -- every time we would get there, we would be given a certain number of bullets. So they saw obviously that I didn't use the bullets, didn't fire them. So they could conclude that I wasn't shooting, there wasn't firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I see. So he reported you. To whom did he report you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He reported me to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And what followed upon -- upon that report being made?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was detained for three days. I was in detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. But I think you said that you had to go to a military court. Do I understand your evidence to be that the report was made, you were taken to this military court, and as punishment you were put into prison for three days?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we object that this is not what he actually stated. He said there was a threat of military court, but not that he actually had to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Perhaps I jumped the gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Perhaps you were just detained for three days without going through a military court. So tell us what the sequence of events. The soldier made the report that you weren't firing and weren't shooting. How -- what happened thereafter to result in your being detained for three days?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was called to go and see the commander, and I was given three days' detention, and I was threatened with the military court, although I did not actually go to appear before a military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So was it the commander who threatened the use of the military court?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And where were you detained for three days?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There, in Brvnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In what? In a room? Were you shackled? What sort of detention are we talking about here?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just a house. I was detained in a room. I presume they made some kind of a prison or a detention room out of it. I'm not sure exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did any of the other men who were in your circumstances, that is, Muslims or Croats who had been ordered to fight, ever suffer similar punishments?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And what sort of punishment was usual? Was it just a question of detention? Or did anything else happen?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Detention. It was detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Apart from actually not shooting, did you do anything else to sabotage the fighting effort of the soldiers with whom you were?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just didn't shoot. I couldn't do anything else personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you believe in the cause of the soldiers whom you had been ordered to fight with?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not believe in it. I did not actually know why they were fighting or whom -- against whom they were fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you ever make any attempt to try and get out of this -- of this requirement to that you fight on behalf of this army?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't have any choice. I couldn't -- I couldn't get out of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours will just bear with me for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. And just before I leave this topic, I want to ask you do you -- can you tell the Chamber if your sentiments that you've just expressed, namely that you didn't want to fight, were shared by other Muslims and Croats who had also been ordered to fight.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume that they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honours. This is speculation, Your Honours. Asking the witness to speculate and to speak about their feelings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. I think that is upheld.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, if Your Honours please, might I just say this -- I in fact wasn't asking the witness to divine the feelings. Perhaps my question came across in that way. What I'm really interested in is had he ever had any information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think you can ask it directly like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Perhaps if I phrase the question like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes I take Defence counsel's point. I think perhaps the question was not phrased properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Let me ask you Mr. Dagovic, this: Did you ever hear from other soldiers -- and by that I mean either Muslim or Croat soldiers who were in your position -- as to whether or not they wished to be there engaged in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear. They did not wish to take part in the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Was this a matter that was discussed from time to time amongst other soldiers in your position?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you also mentioned on the last occasion your eventual exit from the former Yugoslavia. You said that you worked -- sorry, that you were soldiered in Bosanski Samac until December 1994. What happened in December 1994 to cause that to finish?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to correct you. I left Bosanski Samac in December 1993, not in December 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you for that. And please continue. How did you come to leave Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left with a false ID card in the Serbian name. I had to pay for it. That was the only way for me to get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How much did you pay?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 500 German marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Who did you pay that money to?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I paid Fadil Topcagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The man who was a member of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How did you know to go to him to get a false ID card?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because Fadil Topcagic worked on this job before me. There were several Croats and Muslims who used him for this purpose, for -- with a false ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Using the false ID, were you able to leave and drive to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, a little clarification, please. Line 22 of page 19. The witness says, "Because Fadil Topcagic worked on this job before me." It's a little bit unclear, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When you used that expression that he worked on the job before you, what were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I meant was that before me, in the same way. He helped several other Muslims and Croats. So they approached him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You mean by providing false ID papers and so on?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: For money? In exchange for money?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So you heard about -- I assume you heard about this and decided to use Mr. Topcagic's services.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said that you eventually were driven to Belgrade. There did you take refuge at a home of relatives?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How long were you hiding out in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there until the end of May 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Was it your intention to get out of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was my intention. My intention was to get out, but I did not have a passport.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Who was to give you a passport?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fadil Topcagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Was that covered by the 500 Deutschmarks or not?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Just the false ID, the ID card cost 500 German marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you have to pay more money to him to get out?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had to pay to him money for a passport -- for the passport in order to get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, I don't want to go into the details of all of this, but did you eventually make an attempt to get out using a false passport?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Was that near the border with Hungary, at some exit point north of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Was that unsuccessful? Were you arrested and were you in prison for a short time for having a false passport?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was arrested and I was imprisoned for ten days in Subotica in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That particular false passport that you were picked up with at the border, was that one supplied by Topcagic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Just very briefly, where did you get that one from, that particular passport?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I received it from another person, from another man.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So if you were picked up with this false passport and had to serve a short prison sentence, how did you eventually make it out?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the end, with the help of my brother, who had some connections in the government where I was going to go, through their lawyer I managed to leave Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Legally.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that during that year up until December 1993 you'd go back home for short periods of rest and recreation -- I'll withdraw that. You said you'd go home for short periods of time. Did you always go back to the family home, the home that you'd lived in as a normal family up until April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When you fled Bosanski Samac with the false ID, did you leave whatever positions were left at the family home?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the family home?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a Serb family moved into the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Throughout that year up until the time that you got the false ID pass from Mr. Topcagic, had you made any more attempts at trying to get out via an exchange?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Who had you approached to try to bring that about?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I approached Mr. Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And what did he say?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What he said -- he said that he'd see, that he'd try and do something. Until I left, there were another maybe ten exchanges, and I was never on any list for an exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did anyone ever explain to you why it was that you were not permitted to be on an exchange or why you weren't chosen to be on an exchange?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never got an explanation why I didn't leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In -- prior to the events of the 16th and the 17th of April and all that happened thereafter, had you had any plans to leave Bosanski Samac or make a life for yourself elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did have plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What were they?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the plan was to leave Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When were you planning to leave Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after the takeover of Bosanski Samac by the members of the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I don't think we quite understand each other, Mr. Dagovic. I'm talking about the period of time before April of 1992, right up until then. Until then, until the men came to your house with the guns and the armed vehicle, did you have any plans, any intentions to leave your life there, to go and live somewhere else? Was that what was in your mind?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not what I was thinking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: However, you soon thereafter developed a desire to leave, did you not, because you were trying to get out via exchanges and even paid money for false IDs. That's a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'd like you to think about what it was that was having an effect on you to cause you to want to leave. Did your brother's arrest have anything to do with it?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did the forced labour that you had to perform have anything to do with it?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it had. Because this was not the life until the 16th of April. People were arrested, imprisoned, mistreated, killed. So this was no longer that life that we had before the 17th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you consider that you had any choice in the matter of whether or not you could go on living in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did have a possibility of choosing, but my family and I, we chose to leave town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before we go into cross-examination, or before other things are discussed, I just wanted to remind the Prosecution and the Defence that according to the indictment, the allegations are limited up to December 1993. In the case of Mr. Simo Zaric, it's up to December 1992. So that any evidence beyond 1992 -- December 1992 for Mr. Simo Zaric and for the rest, any evidence after December 1993 will be disregarded, so that the Defence doesn't -- don't have to raise any matters in cross-examination unless it is quite connected to the events prior to those two dates. Yes. On second thoughts, I think we can proceed with cross-examination, see if we can clear the witness. Who will start? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dagovic, before this Chamber, you stated that in the course of your stay in Samac in 1992, you had certain work obligations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that between that, you were working on the digging of trenches, connecting corridors, and building of bunkers.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Could we agree that you were doing the work in the place called Grebnica?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what this work obligation involved?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had to dig bunkers, to make bunkers for the members of the army and to dig the trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, members of which army?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the so-called VRS, Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us how far Grebnica is far away from Bosanski Samac, if you can tell us that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's about 5 to 6 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you also tell us that according to you there was a demarcation line before. Could you tell us -- there was a demarcation line.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Chamber who was on the other side of that line.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were members of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In the period while you were doing your military -- your work obligation there, was there an exchange of fire?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: From both sides?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also you did similar work in a village called Zasevice; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us how far away is the village of Zasevice, from Samac?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of work did you do there?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same as in Grebnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Was there a demarcation line there?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us who was on the other side?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you be so kind as to tell us what work did you do in the place of Prud.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not Prud. That was in Bosanski Samac on the bridge that was on the border with Prud. I also dig -- dig there. We made bunkers, and we made some --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please put his microphone on.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We made some -- there was just the river Bosna that flows between these two.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Was there also an exchange of fire there?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Was there mortar fire? Artillery fire?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was gunfire, so from guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you also be so kind as to tell us whether you did a similar kind of work in Brvnik.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us again how far is Brvnik from Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately 10 kilometres, perhaps a little less. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: You also worked there on the digging of trenches and connecting corridors; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And there was a demarcation line there.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Who was on the other side?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Could we then establish that Bosanski Samac in that period, in 1992, was surrounded in a blockade?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say it was surrounded, not under the blockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Surrounded by whom? By the Croatian Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, they were in their own place. They didn't surround Samac, [Realtime transcript read in error "Alija Izetbegovic"] as you say. They were in their own locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dagovic, you also said in your statement that you knew many people in Samac, particularly people who in the course of 1992 they were doing work obligation like you.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Counsel, we are having a problem with the record because you are not pausing after the answer of the witness and the witness is also not pausing before answering the question. The interpreters cannot keep up.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear the question or shall I repeat?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone else out of those people do any digging of trenches, connecting trenches, et cetera, in different locations apart from those we've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean "these couple of locations"?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I mean Grebnica, Zasavica, Prud, Brvnik?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims worked in other places too, not only in Zasavica and Brvnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us which?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They worked in the direction of Gradac, Brcko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Vukovic. I wonder if we could get a little clarification, page 28, line 3; just after the interpreters had said they had a problem. And we have an answer which reads, "Sir, they were in their own place. They didn't surround Samac, Alija Izetbegovic you said" -- I'm uncertain as to why we have a mention of Alija Izetbegovic, whether that's just an error or what. It doesn't seem to make too much sense to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume it's an error in interpretation. None of us mentioned Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. I think we've clarified this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note. Actually counsel's question was missed completely by the court reporter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you worked during the day and you would return in the evening to a flat in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, then, was Samac shelled in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Did that happen often?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you a tricky question perhaps. Did anyone of your family get killed during the shelling?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Your uncle didn't get killed?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain how?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in a camp in Bosanski Samac. He was detained in the SUP building. A shell hit the building, and that's how he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: You also stated in your testimony that you were mobilised, as you put it, into the VRS.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that you were not willing to shoot at your brother, your family, and your friends; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And that is why you spent three days in detention.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you shoot after all when you got out of detention?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very little. And when I did, I shot in the air. I didn't shoot at the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: So we can agree that after those three days of detention, you were not detained again.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: So we can agree that you did use guns after that.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I shot into the air, not at the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dagovic, you gave a statement to the OTP on the 12th of September, 1994.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: You have a brother named Esad Dagovic.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: After leaving Yugoslavia, did you contact your brother Esad in the foreign country where he was living then?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to him before giving the statement to the investigators? Did you talk about anything concerning events in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when your brother gave a statement to this Tribunal or testified?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: You gave your statement on the 12th of September, whereas your brother gave his statement on the 6th and 7th of September.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may well be. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you and your brother give your statements together in the same place?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dagovic, do you know that your father also gave a statement to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Just one thing: Mr. Dagovic, do you know that your brother used to be a member of the units of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that you were not willing to shoot at your own brother?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said that, I meant it in general terms. I didn't want to shoot at my parents, my friends, my brother, my people. I didn't mean my brother personally. I meant all Muslims and Croats, and that was the context.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: While you were forcibly mobilised, did you receive a remuneration of any kind?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did get some sort of remuneration in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in what intervals and how much approximately?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember how much, but it was perhaps every other month that we got some money.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Your brother, Esad, gave -- testified before this Tribunal last year. You know that.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to him before you came here about anything related to the events in Samac and relating to his testimony or statement?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to any international organisation before testifying?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps seek asylum?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: When doing so, did you give any statements relating to events in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: To whom?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I think it was to this International Tribunal for War Crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: When seeking asylum, you gave a statement to the International Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Next counsel? Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could you bear with me for one second while I collect all the documents. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Dagovic. My name is Aleksandar Lazarevic. I am an attorney, and I represent the Defence team of Mr. Simo Zaric for the purpose of your cross-examination and on behalf of that Defence team, I will conduct it on my own. I will be asking you some questions formulated in such a way as to allow you to answer them with a "yes", "no", or "I don't know" so that we go through this as quickly as we can without wasting the precious time of the Trial Chamber. If by any chance you don't understand a question, please let me know, and I will rephrase it so as to be perfectly clear and concise. For the benefit of the interpreters and to avoid a problem that we had during the cross-examination by my colleague, Mr. Vukovic, please wait for the question to be interpreted. You can see the typing on the monitor. And when you see the typing has finished, you can start answering. We need to avoid overlapping. Before I put to you my first question, I would like on behalf of my client, Mr. Zaric, to express his personal regret over the difficult and ugly things that you had -- you and your family had to go through during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, if you don't mind, I will start. Mr. Dagovic, when you were examined by my learned friends from the Prosecution, you noticed perhaps that a topic has recurred very often, and that topic is the 4th Detachment. I would like to ask you a couple of questions regarding the 4th Detachment that my learned friend Mr. Di Fazio omitted in his examination. Do you know when the 4th Detachment was established?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was established before the 17th of April, but I don't know when exactly. I think it was a couple of months before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. But could you be more precise. Was it perhaps the end of 1991 or the beginning of 1992, if you know.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The 4th Detachment was part of the Yugoslav People's Army, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dagovic, in 1991, more precisely in the end of that year, the Yugoslav People's Army was the only military force in the entire territory of the former Yugoslavia. I'm asking you again, was the 4th Detachment at the time when it was established part of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dagovic, do you know what the 17th Tactical Group is?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dagovic, you have never seen a list of the members of the 4th Detachment in black and white, all the members?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I really don't want us to be misunderstood. We have a double negation here, and I want to avoid any inclarities. You never saw such a list.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Nor have you seen a list of members of staff of the 4th Detachment, that is, the list of commanding officers?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You have also never seen a line-up of all the members of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Nevertheless, there was a certain number of Muslims, Croats, and members of other ethnic groups that resided before the war in the territory of Samac in the 4th Detachment; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dagovic, do you know a person by the name of Radovan Antic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether he held a rank in the reserve forces of the JNA or held a position in the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the rank, but I know he was a member of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that it was he who was the commander of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Jovo Savic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Since you answered no, I suppose it makes no sense to ask you whether you know that he was deputy commander of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In response to the questions put to you by my learned friends from the Prosecution, when you identified the persons present here you said you knew Simo Zaric and that you knew him, although not particularly closely, even before the outbreak of the conflict in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You also know - and I don't think that is disputed - that he, too, is a member of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what rank he held? We're now talking about military rank.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about his rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Would you be surprised if I told you that he was a sergeant?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that I didn't know anything about his rank, so I wouldn't be surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that his job was called deputy commander for security, morale, and information in the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, Simo Zaric was the commander of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that topic, sir. I was now sharing the information that we have about his position, his official position in the 4th Detachment. And you told me that you didn't know about it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I have now asked you a number of questions, and you answered a lot of them by saying you didn't know, that you had never seen a line-up of the members, that you had never seen a list, that you didn't know who Jovo Savic was, that you didn't know the ranks held by certain persons. And nevertheless in your statement to the Prosecution, you maintain that Simo Zaric was the commander of the 4th Detachment. Would I be right in saying that it is only your assumption and not something that you know firsthand?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not my assumption. That's the truth, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let us deal with the 4th Detachment for a while longer. When testifying here, you mentioned the names of certain individuals whom you believed to be members of the 4th Detachment, specifically two persons. The first being Mile Zoranovic. And in response to a question by the Prosecutor, you said that he was a member of the 4th Detachment, page 7219 in the transcript -- and Dragan Tubonjic, page 7195, line 11. Let us start with Mr. Tubonjic. My colleague already asked you something about your statement given to the OTP on the 12th September 1994. Do you know which statement I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that at this moment, since -- the best way to go quickly through this would be that I read one sentence of this statement given to the investigators of the OTP, and at that moment my colleagues from the Prosecution can confirm that this statement actually exists -- this portion of statement actually exists, and then I can continue instead of showing him this and making this, two versions, one on ELMO or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, that is the statement of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the statement of this witness given --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we can adopt that procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I think that that is the fastest way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, why can't Mr. Lazarevic simply ask the witness if he said that -- if that's his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes I just want the confirmation from my colleagues that this portion actually is in the statement, that the statement contains this portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio that is not a problem. You can just confirm, because you have the same statement, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It is actually on page 2, last paragraph, from the beginning. And it states here: "My brother was arrested on 5 May 1992 by four men from the SUP. One of the men was Dragan Tugonjic (Tugonja), and the three others I didn't know."

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dagovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If my colleagues could confirm that it is actually in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's what I read here, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Although there is a slight difference in only one letter in the name of this person, a "G" instead of a "B" in the last name of Tugonjic, we are talking about the same person who came with another three men and arrested your brother; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: According to that statement of yours, those four men were from the SUP, which means they were policemen; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came from the SUP. That much is true. But Dragan Tubonjic was a member of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I have discussed this with my client, who undoubtedly was a member of the 4th Detachment. And we've run some checks through our investigators. And my client maintains firmly that Dragan Tubonjic was not a member of the 4th Detachment for a single day. He was rather a member of the police force under the command of Stevan Todorovic, chief of police. And that seems to be indicated in your statement. You said they had come from the SUP and that you had seen them in front of the SUP building. So how do you conclude that he was not a policeman but the member of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he came wearing camouflage uniform. At that time policemen also wore camouflage uniform, but they were blue. And it's correct that Dragan Tubonjic was assigned to the SUP after this incident. But until then, he was a member of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I think we will have to discuss these uniforms a bit more. But let us now go to the second person I've mentioned, Mile Zoranovic. Is that the man nicknamed Mile Pancir? Is that the man?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That is the man who took you to work sites and back, when you performed your work obligation.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And as you put it, he guarded you there.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now, about this gentleman, Mile Zoranovic. There is a sentence in the statement you gave to the investigators of the OTP which caught my attention, caught my eye.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: For my colleagues from the Prosecution, it is also on page 2 of his statement from September 12, 1994, paragraph third, and it states: "He wore a uniform, as all the Serbs did once the war started."

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From this sentence, I understood that when the war began, all Serbs started wearing uniforms. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all Serbs did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: But not all Serbs though were members of the 4th Detachment; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: There were people who had other duties and assignments, not military assignments, and they too wore uniforms; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So solely on the basis of the fact that somebody was wearing a uniform, we cannot conclude that he was a member of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, Bosanski Samac is a very small place. And all members of Serb ethnicity who lived in Bosanski Samac were members of the 4th Detachment. And they spoke about it publicly. It was an open secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So your opinion, your viewpoint, is that all men of military age, able-bodied men, all Serbs after the conflict broke out, they were members of the 4th Detachment. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not what I said. I'm not saying that they were all members of the 4th Detachment. That's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Sir uniforms were worn by the guards as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before -- before you proceed, I think we better correct this with the witness, because the transcript does show what he is now disputing. It says: "And all members of the Serb ethnicity who lived in Bosanski Samac were members of the 4th Detachment." That is on page 41, line 1 and 2 and 3. So perhaps I can ask the witness. What did you mean? Were all the Serbs wearing military uniforms, and is that your position that all of them were members of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. They were not all members of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you -- what is the correct position, then? What is your evidence on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, all Serbs who lived in the town, they were all members of the 4th Detachment. But not all Serbs who lived in the municipality of Bosanski Samac. Because around Samac, there were a lot of Serb villages and not all of them were members of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Counsel, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I think maybe it is a time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take our break and continue at 16.15 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic, you can continue cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dagovic, we had an interruption here. We had a break. And that was at the time when we were discussing the ethnicity of the members of the 4th Detachment. That is, we discussed whether -- whether there were Serbs in other ethnicities, members of the 4th Detachment. And now when I look at the transcript more closely, I would like to ask for a clarification, whether I had understood correctly whether there was a misunderstanding here. Perhaps my question is to blame. We were talking about the town of Samac and the municipality of Samac. So what you're saying is that all citizens of the town of Samac who were Serbs, of Serb ethnicity, they were members of the 4th Detachment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And that the inhabitants of the surrounding Serb villages they were in some other detachments?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I believe this is what the witness had in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So Mr. Dagovic, we will certainly agree that during the war in Samac there were people of Serb ethnicity who worked in factories, who worked in the municipality, who worked in various other places. Were they also members of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now, if we go back to Mr. Mile Pancir, according to my information he worked for the Ministry of Defence. Does that mean also that he was a member of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not work for the Ministry of Defence. Mr. Zoranovic was a member of the 4th Detachment. The information that you have is that he is now working for the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, when was the 4th Detachment disbanded?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If I can help you perhaps, considering that you're the first witness in the case of the Prosecutor -- and I believe that you will probably remain the only one -- who was at some point a member of the VRS from December of 1992. At that time when you became a member of the VRS, that is, in December 1992, was the 4th Detachment in existence?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So you were a member of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In December 1992.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I was not a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And could you tell me, what was the army unit that you belonged to?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were -- it was called the 2nd Battalion, which was -- which was positioned in this line in Brvnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The 5th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 5th Battalion was positioned in Grebnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In the 2nd Battalion, who was your commanding officer?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cvijetin Maslic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you know who was the commander of the 5th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
