utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you practically worked there to meet the needs of the farms themselves.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So you did whatever needed to be done for the farms.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, earlier on in the proceedings, we introduced a document marked D33/3, albeit only in the B/C/S version. Now we have it in English as well, and we would like to avail ourselves of this opportunity to make it available to the Trial Chamber and to show the document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I don't know if my learned friend has noted the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't know if my learned friend has noted the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: This might be an appropriate moment to deal with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. We will take a break and resume our proceedings at 18.10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you can proceed, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dagovic, will you please take a look at this document. I suppose you haven't seen it before.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the document, and then I'll ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Counsel, I want to find out -- when you say you should read the document -- oh, you want him to read it to himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, to himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then I'll ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have, although it's very difficult to make out the words. It's very illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Take the document which is on the ELMO. It's a better copy.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you read out loud the highlighted portion at the top.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Ministry of national defence section, Bosanski Samac."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand correctly, this is a letter addressed to the section of the Ministry of national defence by the secretariat for the economy.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Read the second highlighted portion.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The sugar beat from these plots of land needs to be harvested, so the Bijeljina sugar refinery wrote to this --"

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Read it to the end?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sugar refinery wrote to this secretariat asking for a work schedule -- work obligation to be assigned to engineer -- I can't make out the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Jovo Krstic. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Jovo Krstic, who is deployed in the 3rd Company, 15th infantry brigade, (previously the 4th Detachment), and who was previously involved in the organisation of sugar beat production and harvesting." Shall I go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In view of the above, please establish a work obligation for the said employee to organise the work in question."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You have heard about the Bijeljina sugar refinery, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It was -- it was state-owned -- public owned at the time.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever do any work on harvesting of sugar beat perhaps?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to know one more thing related to this letter. This Jovo Krstic, do you know the man?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This part which says who is deployed in the 3rd Company of the 5th Infantry Battalion, is that the battalion commanded by Mladen Radovic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It says "previously the 4th Detachment."

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can I perhaps refresh your memory by a question asked by my colleague Mr. Lazarevic. Was the 4th Detachment perhaps renamed into the 5th Battalion, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that the 4th Detachment was ever renamed into the 5th Battalion. I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But having seen this document, can you perhaps cast your mind back a little.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document doesn't tell me anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the date.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 25th September 1992 -- 21st September, correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I have finished with this document. If there are no objections, I would like to tender it as an exhibit, because we only had the B/C/S version so far?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Because the witness did say he doesn't know it. He hasn't seen it so far. So anyway, the Prosecution, what was your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, we don't want to object to the full admission of the document; however, for what it's worth, it seems to me that there's not much evidence surrounding the actual document itself. It's a matter that we will be greater able to evaluate. But as far as its full admission is concerned, no, we don't have any objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Can we have the number, please, as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the B/C/S version will be D33/3 ter, and the English translation D33/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, counsel, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to take you back to one topic that was covered in the examination-in-chief. That is the event that occurred when your mother was exchanged and you too expected to be exchanged but you weren't. They were calling out names outside the bus.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Was it one or more buses?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was one or two buses. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe I misunderstood you. You will tell me if that is so. It was mainly women, children, and elderly men whose names were called out.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Was there perhaps another bus which had brought detainees from Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bus for the prisoners was not outside the secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So on that occasion when your mother was exchanged, you were doing your work obligation.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you were a conscript since you were mobilised immediately after that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if you have learnt firsthand or heard from someone, that in order for able-bodied men who were involved in work obligation or military duty to leave Samac they needed an approval from the military command?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you need some sort of consent or approval from them when you were leaving Samac?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And when you were going on leave from the army, who did you ask for permission?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you were on the front line and then you were allowed to go and leave after a while, who did you ask for permission to go home for your own private purposes?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask anyone. If you were there for 48 hours, you automatically were able to take 48 hours off. That was the way it was -- it went. You didn't have to ask anyone for permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, if Your Honours please -- I'm not objecting, but a few questions further up my learned friend put to the witness or said to the witness: "If able-bodied men who were involved in work obligation or military duty needed approval from the military command to leave Bosanski Samac." I'm not sure if my learned friend was putting to the witness in order to get out via an exchange you needed permission from a military -- a military command or whether just to leave the town. That might be important. And if there is -- if my learned friend is trying to make some point around that, then perhaps that issue ought to be clarified, because it wasn't clear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will divide this issue into two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in order to be exchanged, in order for military conscripts and people involved in the work brigade to be exchanged, the approval was necessary from the competent military command?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And did you know at that time in that period when you were in Bosanski Samac that in order to leave Bosanski Samac, which was engulfed by the conflict, military conscripts and men involved in the work brigade or under work obligation needed approval from the competent authority in the national defence department?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. I have completed my cross-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes before you sit down, you were giving these two other photographs which you haven't discussed, so we will return them to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I will need them for another witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I'll take them back and tender them again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. Actually, they were not tendered. They were not discussed by the witness. So you can have them back. Ms. Baen, any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Re-examination by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You were asked some questions about the remuneration that you received while working -- sorry, fighting. You were paid. Did you receive the same pay as everyone else in the army for which you were fighting?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if we got the same remuneration as Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Would Your Honours just bear with me for one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You were asked questions about the role of Mr. Zaric in the 4th Detachment. And Defence counsel put to you that you were assuming that Simo Zaric was the commander of the 4th Detachment, not something that you knew firsthand. And you said, "No, that's not my assumption. It's the truth." On what basis do you assert that the truth is that Simo Zaric was the commander of the 4th Detachment? In other words, what do you know or what did you see or what did you hear that makes you say the truth of the matter is that Simo Zaric was the commander of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the 4th Detachment said so publicly. And when there was a gathering at the memorial hall, Mr. Zaric introduced himself as the commander of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Are you referring to the meeting at the Spomen Dom hall where the issue of mobilisation or the indication of mobilisation was raised?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I understood your evidence in cross-examination to be that the prohibition against the assembly of two or three persons of Muslim or Croat ethnicity occurred in this way: First there was an announcement on the radio, and later in time you saw posters around the town to the same effect. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: About what period of time would you say separated the radio announcement from your first sighting of the posters?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown D36/3. That's the photograph that was tendered this afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Using the marker, can you -- the pointer, that instrument that you have there, can you just show us where you would assemble in the morning, where the workers would assemble in the morning.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would be standing here outside the building. We waited for our assignments to forced labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: For the purposes of the transcript, can the -- can it be reflected that the witness indicated the area in front of the building facing the road at a point at which it can be seen a small dark green car. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You were also asked --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher. I've finished with that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You were also asked questions regarding a paragraph that had been -- regarding a certain paragraph in your statement regarding the role of Bozo Ninkovic in issuing instructions in relation to forced labour. That was part of the statement. I want to read a certain portion of the statement to you, and tell me -- could you tell me if you agree that this was part of your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: This is the statement dated ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The statement dated the 12th of September, 1994, referred to by Defence counsel earlier this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: They read a portion of the paragraph. I think it's fair that the witness be able to put that phrase or sentence into context and that the whole paragraph be read. And that's all I want to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And this is the paragraph that I want to read to you. So just follow it -- follow what I'm reading out to you, Witness, please. "I know that Stevan Todorovic or Stiv was the chief of the SUP. Before the war, he worked in a plant --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object. My reading of -- a portion of the statement was only directed to the work obligation. And that part of the witness's statement where he mentioned people in charge of issuing work obligations was the only part I read, and that's when we mentioned Bozo Ninkovic. I didn't mention any other detail in my cross-examination and I don't think it is appropriate for the Prosecutor to come back to it, because that was not one of the topics I raised in my cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Certainly. The portion that I'm going to read will touch upon the -- the sort of functions performed by other people, including some of these defendants. However, the paragraph was dealing with what this witness asserted was people in power. And it only dealt with the aspect of Bozo Ninkovic's activities, as far as this witness's assertion of who those people in power were. So from that point of view, I think they should be put into context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Trial Chamber will allow the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll continue reading to you, referring to Todorovic, you continue. "He came to the Rendezvous restaurant frequently. He became the chief after the war. He gave most of the orders, even when my brother was imprisoned. Other people in charge were Blagoje Simic, president of Bosanski Samac municipality; Mladen Radovic, commander of the 5th Battalion (Roda) for Bosanski Samac: Bozo Ninkovic, chief representative of the Ministry of Defence of Bosanski Samac for the Serbs. He was also the one who was in charge of giving the work orders for the forced labour. I know that he was the one giving the orders because he gave orders to the people picking us up for work. They always had a piece of paper with his signature on it. It was widely known that these people were in charge along with Simo Zaric. I didn't have to see it because everyone knew that Stiv was ordering arrests along with Blagoje Simic and Simo Zaric." Now, what I want to ask you is this: Were you there describing people who in your opinion, in your view, were in charge in Bosanski Samac during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When you say that Bozo Ninkovic was the man giving orders to the people in regards of work obligation, forced labour, is your statement to be read as being -- as saying that that's all he exerted control or had power over? I'm talking about Bozo Ninkovic.

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You mentioned also the topic of the distribution of milk and bread for a period of two weeks after the outbreak of hostilities. Who was distributing that milk and bread?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I think this was distributed by the members of the Red Cross. I don't know who was in charge of that. I'm not sure about it. In fact, the important thing is it was distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you manage to get some milk and bread yourself?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on a couple of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And that distribution ceased after a period of two weeks; is that your position?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did it ever resume again, or was that the end of it?

utterances.speaker: SAFET DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I have no further re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Dagovic. You can leave the courtroom. You are now released, and you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any other witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, if Your Honours please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I recall what was discussed before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So if there is no witness available, that's the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. We can move on to our discussion on the possibility of --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, 92 bis. Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, I've prepared for that. May I just have a moment to gather my papers which I had to shift earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I just provide the Chamber with these three -- this document. It's in -- I've got -- provided Defence counsel with copies. This is purely an aid to my submission. It can be disposed of after I've finished making my submission. It's purely to assist the Chamber in following what I have to say. It's not a document that needs to be entered into evidence or anything like that. You see from that document, Your Honours, that we have some 30 witnesses left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The witnesses in group 1, Kemal Mehinovic, Witness E, Hajrija Drljacic, and Witness C are what I call impending witnesses. They're about to come and give evidence. In fact, Mehinovic is booked to fly in from the United States today. She -- the Witness E is booked to come in, in six days' time, and he'll be flying in from a European country. And Hajrija Drljacic is coming in on the 10th of this month. It -- in the Prosecution's submission, given the immediacy and -- sorry, and I should also mention Witness C. He's also coming in on the 10th of this month. Given the impending arrival of this particular witnesses, it would be just impractical for the Prosecution to even try to get statements from these particular witnesses in the form of -- that would be -- would suit the provisions of Rule 92 bis. And so we say we can't do anything in that respect. Group 2 consists of a number of witnesses that the Chamber has not indicated via a letter I received from -- a letter that was caused to be sent to me, I understand, from the Registry. Those particular witnesses are not included. And so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You mean the letter from the legal officer?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's right. Yes. I think that's the correct term, yes. The letter from the -- yes, the legal officer. They are not included on that list, and so therefore I assume that the Trial Chamber has not suggested that we try to deal with those witnesses pursuant to the provisions of Rule 92 bis. And may I say respectfully, they are the sort of witnesses, I think, that we should deal with in the normal way. I'll deal with group 3 in just a moment. Group 4 consists of three witnesses. Ewa Tabeau is a witness in the usual way, but the Prosecution has taken on board what you have said regarding the speed of the trial and the need to hasten it. If she is to give any evidence at all in chief, it will be very, very brief, extremely brief. She has prepared a report that's been provided to the Defence, and the only examination-in-chief that would be elicited from her would be just tidying up aspects or explaining one or two aspects of her report, and it is not intended that she would take a long time, as far as the examination-in-chief is concerned. How long it would take in cross-examination, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yeah. This is a problem we've been having in other trials as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: On experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: An expert will give in the report, which is -- which will be produced and the CV. There is no need for viva voce evidence because it is an opinion of the expert, and then the expert is presented for cross-examination where the Defence has indicated -- as in this case they have indicated. So we don't want anything already in the report being discussed orally. If there is any addition that has to be made, then you better get the additional statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Well, we could deal with that in that way. Do Your Honours -- do Your Honours' comments extend as far as cross-examination of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, not cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm talking about examination-in-chief, where we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: An opinion already.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In that case, I understand that. If there are matters of clarification, we could deal with it by way of an additional statement and clarify anything in the report that we feel needs to be done. That can be attended to fairly -- fairly quickly. So in effect, that particular witness would only be -- having now heard what you have to say about that, only in -- given evidence as far as cross-examination is concerned. The other two witnesses in relation to international armed conflict, they are already the subject of a 92 bis order. They will be coming in for cross-examination only. There will be no evidence led by -- from them by the Prosecution. Group 6 consists of four witnesses. As I indicated, we have conducted a review of the Prosecution witnesses, and in an effort to get the trial moving, bring about the close of the Prosecution case, the Prosecution is minded to withdraw those witnesses from the list altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That is group 6. 27, 28, 29, 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think let's have the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Zvonko Susak, Sead Mujkanovic, Muharem Jasarevic, and Witness F.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So these are no longer going to be called by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes now, that should have in the Prosecution's submission a substantial effect on the time required for the Prosecution case. Group 5, witnesses that the Prosecution submits would be appropriate to be dealt with by the provisions of Rule 92 bis. As far as number 26 is concerned, he is a witness who is in ill health and the Chamber has already indicated that -- I think the Prosecution has indicated to the Chamber and the Chamber has reacted favourably I believe to a suggestion that his evidence be taken by way of videolink. He is a man who suffers kidney problems and has to have dialysis three times a week. He can't be far from his machine. And the only practical way of getting his evidence would be via videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I would have thought he would be the most suitable under Rule 92 bis and then we have videolink for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That might -- that might indeed hasten the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes then he will spend very little time in the witness box.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. That's true. Yes. I understand that. It would also mean having to get a Registry officer to go down to Bosnia to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Swear the statement and make sure all the proper procedures are adhered to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That will -- that will mean for the Prosecution to do that, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- the -- the very serious concern here is the length of time the trials are taking.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So that is why there is emphasis on if use of Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, I appreciate that, Your Honours. So that will be six witnesses in addition dealing -- to be dealt with by way -- by utilising the provisions of Rule 92 bis. So we turn then to group 3. They are witness that is the Prosecution would like to deal with -- to have dealt with in the normal way. I can tell you something about those particular witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All of them - all of them - are witnesses who gave their statements years ago. Of those particular witnesses, two of them gave statements in 1994; five of them gave statements in 1995; and three of them provided statements which have not been signed -- in other words, formally accepted by those particular witnesses. They are statements that were taken before the rule was in existence. They are statements which were taken without the rule and the provisions of the rule being considered by the statement taker. They are statements that were taken in ignorance of many of the exhibits in this particular case. They are statements that don't deal with much of the documentary evidence in this particular case. And they are statements that were taken at a time when the trial issues have not crystallised as they have over the last few months. Because of that, the Prosecution would not be happy in simply producing the statements as they -- as they stand, simply getting the witness to come along and adopt the procedures in Rule 92 bis, formalise them, and we simply hand them in, because they simply don't come to grips with the sorts of issues that we've been dealing with and have arisen as the important issues, even on background material in this trial. That means we would have to take statements again from them and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I thought that the provisions of Rule 92 bis have got specific requirements that have to be fulfilled.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And it would mean taking statements under 92 bis, not using those statements which were recorded by the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, precisely. I understand that if that were to happen, the sort of procedure that would have to be adopted is this: One of the team members -- Prosecution team members would have to take the statement. If -- and I say that because we can't -- we can't leave the task to someone else because of the fact that we're so far into the trial and the three Prosecutors are well aware of each --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All the issue that is have arisen, even on the background matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And the Prosecution feel that is in order to put -- present the evidence in the best possible way, one of us -- one of the three, my colleague Mr. Weiner, my colleague Ms. Reidy or myself would have to engage in that task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Experience has shown in proofing witnesses here that that takes around two days at least, if not two and a half day or three, and sometimes up to three days of fairly solid work. That means that it would be a big drain on the Prosecution in sending Prosecutors down to Bosnia, if that were to happen. But whatever happens, whether the statement is taken in Bosnia or whether the statement is taken here, there's going to then follow a period of some delay. The statement will have to be put into proper shape and form. It will have to be translated. I've made inquiries of various people in the know as to what sort of backlog or period of time is required for translation. I can't seem to get a clear answer, and I think people in the translation services have indicated there's a good reason for that, and that is that it just -- there never is a specific period of time required for translation in the normal course of events. It's not always the case that there's a four-week backlog or a two-week -- a two-day backlog or whatever. It changes from time to time. My case manager informs me that as a customer of the services and a man handing in documents, that realistically if you can get a document certified or designated or considered as a high priority document, it will take four to five days. If it goes through in the normal course of events, it will take a longer period of time. So that will add a period of time to -- once the statement is taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Then the statement has to be sworn and the usual procedures --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes the procedures are there under 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Under Rule 92 bis. And that has to be done. Then the statement has to be provided to the Defence, who under the rule have a period of two weeks -- two weeks' grace. Sorry, I should phrase it this way: Under the rule, under Rule 92(E), have a period of -- or rather, the Prosecution would have to give them a period of two weeks' notice before the statement can be used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes that is -- that is in a situation where the matters are not being discussed in the presence of the Defence. And that is in a situation where there haven't been any previous brief summaries, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That is why that rule is provided, and there is nothing to stop the Trial Chamber to bridge that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. I can see -- I realise that, from looking at the rules, and you can avail yourselves of further provision under Rule 127 and vary that time. Having spoken to some Defence counsel, in particular Mr. Lukic, I understand that the Defence could like that two-week period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Well, the -- the Trial Chamber will have to make a ruling on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because the Defence will have to convince the Trial Chamber that they have no knowledge at all of this evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes so the scenario is in practical terms, if you get a witness here or if we go down to Bosnia, there's going to be some period time -- and I just can't say how -- what sort of period time -- after for translation to occur, for service -- for delivery and service of the statement on the Defence, and then of course a period of time, if they get it, for them to digest the material and make whatever inquiries that I want and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So there will be a period of time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: This is -- all those points, Mr. Di Fazio, is being looked into by the Trial Chamber. And I'm sure that the Defence counsel know that where they've already had an indication of whatever evidence the particular witness will give, it will even serve them better to have a full statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Leaving out, of course, what is accepted under Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So the question of them having time to prepare for the cross-examination will not arise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That still leaves the period of the translation to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Because the other thing we can do is to swap the witnesses. We don't have to follow this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Oh, this is not an order of witnesses. This is just the category --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The category of witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: This is definitely not an order of witnesses at all. It's just a category

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So the upshot is that out of the 30 witnesses, we've gotten rid of four, added six -- that's ten. That's a third of those witnesses whose evidence we propose to take utilising the provisions of Rule 92 bis. And essentially that would leave the 17 that you see on the first page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: -- to give evidence in the normal fashion. Out of those 17, there's really nothing that we can do with the first four, in any event, simply from the term -- point of view of practicalities and time constraints and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes, the Trial Chamber can see that. So that group 1 and group 2, roughly indicated by the Prosecution, we can continue with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And then group 3 and group 5, they should go under Rule 92 bis without fail. And then we can have group 4 witnesses brought forward --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- in order for the time you are discussing of going to collect the statements under Rule 92 bis. If this was done, really it would cut down on the hours we spend in court --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- collecting -- receiving evidence viva voce.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. You understand, Your Honours, that group 3 is the witnesses that the Prosecution wishes to call in the normal fashion; in other words, full examination in the way that we've been going so far and full cross-examination. In other words, the usual procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. I thought group 3 witnesses were the ones you were discussing about them having given their statements 1994, 1995. And also the Trial Chamber is aware that it is possible under Rule 92 bis to have partly statement, partly oral.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. So it's a question of the Prosecution reorganising this group 3 and adding them on to -- adding them to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Your Honour slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The interpreters. I'm too fast. So the Prosecution has to reorganise group 3 witnesses, group 5 witnesses, and put them under 92 bis fully or partially, as the rule provides, and then we can bring forward group 4 witnesses. These are the experts, the witness on international armed conflict, the witness on international armed conflict - the other one again - forward, for whom it appears to the Trial Chamber the statements are already ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So that by the time we finish Kemal Mehinovic, Witness E, Hajrija Drljacic, Witness C most of this work will have been done for group 3 witnesses and group 5 witnesses to -- for -- where the Prosecution has to get the statements recorded under Rule 92 bis. And then we have group 2 as well, who will still be coming along in the normal way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. There's some nine witnesses in group 3, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: We -- getting approval for missions and getting down there would -- it -- to start the process of proofing and getting the statements from these people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: There is no problem, Mr. Di Fazio. All you do is put the machinery in motion. That's all. And one of you has to go down there and get the -- the statements recorded. It's a question of asking the Registrar to appoint a presiding officer. And this is what the Tribunal actually in almost all cases is trying to embark on, to cut down on hearing time, to get the trials completed as soon as possible, so that the detainees waiting for their trials can have their trials commenced. So there is nothing new that you are discussing, Mr. Di Fazio, that hasn't happened in other cases. It's a question of reorganising and getting the work done and then bringing group 4 witnesses forward, like I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sure the Defence are following -- they've got the document, so they know the names of the witnesses involved so that there will be no confusion at a latter stage as to which witness we are discussing for which procedure. And also the suggestion of the Trial Chamber must be marked that the witnesses in group 4 numbered 18, 19, and 20, will have to be brought forward. So I want the Defence to prepare themselves for cross-examining these witnesses if need be at an earlier stage than otherwise has been indicated before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll convey your remarks to those instructing me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The Prosecution has heard what the Chamber has to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecutor is very, very keen to have the trials going, as you can see from the amount of work she herself is doing in getting those who are not arrested arrested and those who are not -- those who are willing to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Because there is capacity for the Tribunal to hold all these trials if we all reorganise ourselves and get the work going. Tomorrow we will proceed with our Variant A and B. I notice that Ms. Reidy was not here, but she was here at the beginning, so she should come.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: She will be available tomorrow at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. And I also note that Ms. Baen is there, because it had been agreed that she was the one -- You are the one taking up this matter. So your submissions will come in tomorrow, and thereafter we will proceed on the rule -- on the Variant A and B as far as we can go tomorrow. All right? And I also just want to note -- that's the language assistant you are sitting with, Ms. Baen? Because I notice that Mr. Zecevic is not here.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Yes. She's our case manager, and she also serves as an interpreter for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I also want to point out to the Defence especially that the Trial Chamber is observing the cross-examination. There may be a time as we go on with the Prosecution case when the Trial Chamber would like to narrow down the issues, so that in areas of the Prosecution where there is no -- it's not -- the facts are not being contested, then we will proceed without cross-examination. So I think the Defence counsel should be looking into that so that should the Trial Chamber decide that we will narrow down the issues -- the contentious matters, then the Defence will be ready with that. So we'll adjourn until tomorrow at 14.15 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: at 7.05 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 2nd day of May, 2002, at 2.15 p.m.
